question.text: In a $12$ -bit computer instruction format, the size of the address field is $3$ bits. question.subject: CO & Architecture

question.text:
The baseline execution time of a program on a single-core machine is $200$ nanoseconds (ns). The code corresponding to $90\%$ of the execution time can be fully parallelised. The overhead for using each additional core is $5$ ns when running on a multicore system. Assume that all cores in the multicore system run their share of the parallelised code for an equal amount of time.

The number of cores that minimise the execution time of the program is $\_\_\_\_$ .
question.subject: CO & Architecture

question.text: An $8$-way set-associative cache memory unit with a capacity of $64$ KB is built using a block size of $16$ words. The word length is $32$ bits. The size of the physical address space is $16$ GB . The number of bits for the TAG field is $\_\_\_\_$
question.subject: CO & Architecture

question.text:
A computer system has an L1 cache, an L2 cache, and a main memory unit. The block size in L2 cache is 16 words. The data bus between the L2 cache and main memory is 4 words wide. The memory access times are 2 nanoseconds, 20 nanoseconds, and 200 nanoseconds for L1 cache, L2 cache, and the main memory unit, respectively.

When there is a miss in both L1 and L2 cache, a block is transferred from main memory to L2 cache. What is the total time taken for this transfer, assuming the bus cycle time is the same as the L2 cache access time?

  1. $80$ nanoseconds
     
  2. $200$ nanoseconds
     
  3. $220$ nanoseconds
     
  4. $280$ nanoseconds
question.subject: CO & Architecture

question.text:
Consider a $2$-way set associative cache (initially empty) with a total of 16 cache blocks. The main memory consists of 256 blocks and the requests for memory blocks are in the following order:
$$0,255,1,4,3,8,133,159,216,129,63,8,48,32,73,92,155$$
Which one of the following memory blocks WILL be in the cache if an LRU replacement policy is used?

  1. $0$
     
  2. $8$
     
  3. $129$
     
  4. $216$
question.subject: CO & Architecture

question.text:
A DMA controller transfers data from an I/O device to main memory using cycle stealing. The CPU is running at a frequency of $50$ MHz . The I/O device transfers data at a rate of $500 \mathrm{~KB} / \mathrm{s}$ (Kilobytes per second). The DMA controller transfers data one word ($4$ bytes) at a time. If one memory cycle takes one CPU clock cycle, what percentage of CPU cycles are stolen by the DMA controller?

  1. $0.256 \%$
     
  2. $2.56 \%$
     
  3. $1.28 \%$
     
  4. $0.128 \%$
question.subject: CO & Architecture

question.text:
An instruction set architecture is implemented using two different processor designs:

 

  • P1: A single-cycle processor with a clock period of $10 \ \text{ns}$ .

  • P2: A multi-cycle processor with a clock period of $2 \ \text{ns}$ .

 

On the multi-cycle processor (P2), instructions are categorized with the following cycle counts:

 

  • ALU instructions: $4$ cycles

  • Load/Store instructions: $5$ cycles

  • Branch instructions: $3$ cycles

 

For a program with an instruction mix of $50 %$ ALU, $25 %$ Load/Store, and $25 %$ Branch instructions, which processor is faster and by what factor?

 

  1. P1 IS FASTER BY A FACTOR OF $1.25$.
     
  2. P2 IS FASTER BY A FACTOR OF $1.25$.
     
  3. P1 IS FASTER BY A FACTOR OF $1.5$.
     
  4. P2 IS FASTER BY A FACTOR OF $1.5$.
question.subject: CO & Architecture

question.text:
In a system where multiple I/O devices are connected using a daisy-chaining scheme for interrupt handling, three devices, D1, D2, and D3 are connected in that order of proximity to the CPU (D1 is closest). If all three devices request an interrupt at the same time, how is the priority resolved?

  1. The device physically farthest from the CPU (D3) gets the highest priority.
     
  2. The CPU polls each device to determine the highest-priority request.
     
  3. The device physically closest to the CPU (D1) gets the highest priority.
     
  4. All requests are serviced in a round-robin fashion.
question.subject: CO & Architecture

question.text:
A C program, which initializes an integer array A of $4096$ elements to zero, is run on a computer with a direct-mapped data cache. The relevant details are provided below:

  • Array Declaration:
     
    int A[4096];

     
  • Element Size: sizeof(int) is $4$ Bytes.
     
  • Cache Size: $44 KBytes.
     
  • Cache Block (Line) Size: $32$ Bytes.
     
  • The cache is initially empty.
     
  • The base address of the array A is $\mathrm{0x00000000}$.

The program executes the following loop:


 

int sum = 0;
for (int i = 0; i < 4096; i = i + 128) {
    sum += A[i];
}


What is the total number of data cache misses generated by this loop?

  1. $8$
     
  2. $16$
     
  3. $32$
     
  4. $128$

question.text:

question.text:
A processor has a $5$-stage instruction pipeline: Instruction Fetch (IF), Instruction Decode (ID), Execute (EX), Memory Access (MEM), and Register Writeback (WB). The clock cycle time is $1$ ns. Assume that the pipeline has no data forwarding mechanism. An instruction's result is written to the register file in the WB stage and can be read by another instruction only in the subsequent clock cycles.

Consider the following sequence of instructions:

I1: ADD R1, R2, R3 (R1 - R2 + R3)
I2: SUB R4, R1, R5 (R4 -R1-R5)
I3: AND R6, R1, R7 (R6 \leftarrow R1 AND R7)
I4: OR R8, R4, R9 (R8 - R4 ORR9)


The total time (in nanoseconds) required to execute this sequence of instructions is $\_\_\_\_\_$ .

question.text:

question.text:
A computer's main memory unit has a peak theoretical bandwidth of $12.8 \mathrm{~GB} / \mathrm{s}$. The memory is constructed using DDR4 SDRAM chips which have the following characteristics:

question.text:

An optimizing compiler for Processor $B$ reduces the instruction count for the same program to $0.75 \times 10^9$ instructions. What is the speedup of Processor B over Processor A for this program?

question.text:
A six-stage pipeline processor has the stages: Fetch (FE), Decode (DE), Register Read (RR), Execute (EX), Memory Access (MA), and Write Back (WB). Each stage takes $1$ clock cycle. The EX stage takes $1$ cycle for SUB instructions and $4$ cycles for DIV instructions. The pipeline uses operand forwarding. question.text:

$$

  2. $8$
     
  3. $9$

question.text:
A processor uses 16-bit instructions and has a byte-addressable memory. It has a post-increment register indirect addressing mode, $\mathrm{(Rx)+}$, which first fetches the operand from the memory location pointed to by $\mathrm{R_x}$ and then increments $\mathrm{R_x}$ by the size of the operand (in this case, $2$ bytes for a $16$ -bit word).

Before executing the instruction $\mathrm{ADD R3, (R1)+}$, the state is as follows:

  • Register $\mathrm{R1= 0 \times 1000}$
     
  • Register $\mathrm{R3 =0 \times 3000}$
     
  • $\mathrm{Memory[0x1000]}$ $=0 \times 20$
     
  • Memory $[0 \times 1001]=0 \times 00$ (So the 16 -bit word at $0 \times 1000$ is $8 \times 2000$ )

Which of the following statements is/are TRUE after the execution of the instruction?

  1. The value in register R3 will be $0 \times 5000$.
     
  2. The instruction performs the operation $\mathrm{R} 3+\mathrm{R} 3+\mathrm{M}[\mathrm{R} 1], \mathrm{R} 1=\mathrm{R} 1+2$.
     
  3. The value in register R1 will be $0 \times 1002$.
     
  4. The value in register R1 will be $0 \times 1001$.
question.subject: CO & Architecture

question.text:
A computer system features a two-level cache. The L1 cache has an access time of $10$ ns and a hit rate of $90 \%$. The L2 cache has an access time of $40$ ns and a local hit rate of $95 \%$ (for misses from L1). The main memory has an access time of $200$ ns. What is the average memory access time (AMAT) for this system?

  1. $15$ ns
     
  2. $34$ ns
     
  3. $13.8$ ns
     
  4. $50$ ns

question.text:
A 16-bit processor uses instructions with the following format:

Opcode (4 bits) | Dst Register (3 bits) | Base Register (3 bits) | Offset (6 bits)


The opcode $0 \times 9$ specifies a LOAD operation that uses indexed addressing. The effective memory address is calculated as:

Effective Address = (Contents of Base Register) + Offset


Consider the instruction word $0 \times 959 \mathrm{~A}$. Before the instruction is executed, the system state is as follows:

 

  • Register R6 contains the value $80$.
  • Memory at address $106$ contains the value $250$ .

What is the value loaded into the destination register after this instruction is executed?

  1. $250$
     
  2. $106$
     
  3. $80$
     
  4. $26$

question.text:
A CPU has a 5-stage pipeline with the following stages: Fetch (F), Decode (D), Execute (E), Memory $(\mathrm{M})$ and Write-back (W). Each stage takes one clock cycle to complete. Assume there are no pipeline stalls and the pipeline is initially empty. How many clock cycles are required to complete the execution of $10$ instructions?

  2. $14$
     
  3. $15$
     
  4. $19$

question.text:
A Computer uses a memory unit with $256$ K words of $32$ bits each. A binary instruction code is stored in one word of memory. The instruction has four parts: an indirect bit, an operation code, a register code part to specify one of $64$ registers and an address part. How many bits are there in the operation code, the register code part and the address part?

The hit rates of Level $1$ and Level $2$ caches are $0.7$ and $0.8$, respectively. What is the average access time of the system if parallel searching is used at all levels?

question.text:
A magnetic disk has the following specifications:

  • Number of recording surfaces $=8$
  • Number of tracks per surface $=20,000$
  • Number of sectors per track = 400
  • Sector size $=1 \mathrm{~KB}$
  • Disk rotation speed $=6000 \mathrm{rpm}$

The disk controller uses cycle stealing DMA mode. In this mode, whenever a byte is ready, it transfers it to memory directly (or reads a byte from memory in case of a write). The memory has a cycle time of $100$ ns.

Assume continuous data transfer is possible once the head is positioned at the beginning of a track.

The maximum fraction of CPU time that can be blocked during a DMA transfer is ____________ $\%$.

question.text:
Consider a $5$-segment pipeline with a clock cycle time of $20$ ns in each sub-operation. Find out the approximate speed-up ratio between a pipelined and non-pipelined system to execute $100$ instructions. (If, on average, every five cycles, a bubble due to data hazard has to be introduced in the pipeline)

  2. $4.03$
     
  3. $4.81$
     
  4. $4.17$

question.text:

question.text:
A particular parallel program computation requires $100$ sec when executed on a single processor. If $40 \%$ of this computation is inherently sequential (i.e., will not benefit from additional processors), then theoretically best possible elapsed times of this program running with 2 and 4 processors, respectively, are

question.text:
Arrange the given steps required for a Direct Memory Access (DMA) transfer in the correct order.

(A) Initiate DMA transfer request

(B) Transfer data directly between peripheral and memory

(C) Processor grants DMA control over the system bus

(D) DMA controller completes data transfer and signals completion

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

  1. $(C), (A), (B), (D)$
     
  2. $(A), (C), (B), (D)$
     
  3. $(A),(B),(C),(D)$
     
  4. $(C), (B), (A), (D)$

  • Instruction Decode (ID): $8$ ns
  • Execute (EX): $10$ ns
  • Memory Access (MEM): $12$ ns
  • Write Back (WB): $7$ ns

This process is implemented in a pipelined processor. Assume a latch delay (buffer overhead) of $1$ ns between each pipeline stage. For a program with $1000$ instructions, $20\%$ of the instructions are found to cause $2$ stall cycles each due to data dependencies.

What is the speedup of this pipelined processor compared to a non-pipelined processor that executes the same instructions?

  3. $2.79$

The possible maximum speedupby this design will be ______. (upto 2 decimal places)

question.text:
Consider two cache organizations. The first is a $128$ KB 4-way set associative cache with a $64$byte block size. The second is of the same size and block size but is direct mapped. The system uses a $40$-bit physical address in both cases.

The component latencies are as follows:

  • A $k$-bit comparator has a latency of $\frac{k}{20} \mathrm{~ns}$.
     
  • An $N$-to-1 multiplexer has a latency of $0.3 \times \log _2(N) \mathrm{ns}$.

The hit latency of the set associative organisation is $h_1$ and that of the direct mapped organisation is $h_2$.

The value of the difference, $h_1-h_2$, is:

  2. $1.85$ ns
     
  3. $1.15$ ns
     
  4. $0.10$ ns

  • L1 cache hit rate is $95 \%$.
     
  • $\quad \mathrm{L} 2$ cache hit time is $20$ ns .
     
  • For misses in $\mathrm{L} 1,90 \%$ are found in the L 2 cache (this is the local hit rate for L 2 ).

question.text:
An instruction pipeline consists of four stages: Fetch (F), Decode (D), Execute (E), and Write-Back (W). Each stage can accommodate only one instruction per clock cycle. The pipeline must process the following five instructions:

\[
\begin{array}{|l|c|c|c|c|}
\hline
\text{Instruction} & \text{Fetch} & \text{Decode} & \text{Execute} & \text{Write-Back} \\
\hline
A & 2 & 1 & 2 & 1 \\
B & 1 & 3 & 1 & 2 \\
C & 2 & 2 & 2 & 2 \\
D & 1 & 1 & 3 & 1 \\
E & 2 & 3 & 1 & 1 \\
\hline
\end{array}
\]

Assume:

  • Only one instruction can occupy a stage at any given clock cycle.
     
  • Instructions must move through stages in order: $\mathrm{F} \rightarrow \mathrm{D} \rightarrow \mathrm{E} \rightarrow \mathrm{W}$.
     
  • No instruction can overtake another.

What is the minimum number of clock cycles required to complete the execution of all five instructions?

question.text: A computer has a cache, main memory, and a disk used for virtual memory. If a referenced word is in the cache, $20$ ns are required to access it. If it is in main memory but not in the cache, $60$ ns are needed to load it into the cache, and then the reference is started again. If the word is not in main memory, $12$ ms are required to fetch the word from disk, followed by $60$ ns to copy it to the cache, and then the reference is started again. The cache hit ratio is $0.9$ and the main memory hit ratio is $0.6$ . The average time in nanoseconds required to access a referenced word on this system is________.

question.text:
Consider a standard 5-stage pipeline CPU.

The CPU executes the following sequence of instructions:

1. I1: LOAD R1, 100(R2) ; R1 $\leftarrow \mathrm{M}[\mathrm{R} 2+100]$

2. I2: ADD R3, R1, R4 ; R3 $\leftarrow \mathrm{R} 1+\mathrm{R} 4$

3. I3: SUB R5, R3, R6 ; R5 $\leftarrow \mathrm{R} 3$ - R6

4. I4: STORE R5, 200(R2) ; $\mathrm{M}[\mathrm{R} 2+200] \leftarrow \mathrm{R} 5$

5. I5: ADD R7, R1, R5 ; R7 $\leftarrow \mathrm{R} 1+\mathrm{R} 5$

Each stage takes exactly one clock cycle. Assume no structural hazards are there.

The total number of clock cycles required to complete the above sequence of instructions, starting from the fetch of I1 is ________.
question.subject: CO & Architecture

question.text:
A uniprocessor system runs at $1$ GHz and is connected to a sensor device that produces $1$ data word every $2 \mu \mathrm{~s}$.

In Programmed I/O, the processor continuously polls the device. To read one word, it first reads the status register, checks if data is ready, then reads the data register, and finally stores the word in memory. Each instruction (read, check, or store) takes $1$ cycle except reading the data register, which takes $3$ cycles. Reading the status register takes $2$ cycles, and checking it takes $1$ cycle.

In Interrupt-driven I/O, the device raises an interrupt whenever data is ready. The interrupt service routine first saves the CPU context ($5$ cycles), then reads the status register, checks the status, reads the data register, and stores the word into memory, and finally restores the CPU context ($5$ cycles). Reading the data register takes $3$ cycles, checking the status takes $1$ cycle, and reading the status register takes $2$ cycles.

Assume the CPU performs useful computation only when it is not servicing I/O. Ignore memory stalls and DMA.

Which of the following statement(s) is/are correct?

  1. Programmed I/O consumes fewer CPU cycles per data word than Interrupt-driven I/O.
     
  2. Interrupt-driven I/O consumes fewer CPU cycles per data word than Programmed I/O.
     
  3. CPU spends more than $1 \%$ of its time servicing interrupts if using Interrupt-driven I/O.
     
  4. CPU spends less than $1 \%$ of its time servicing I/O if using Programmed I/O.
question.subject: CO & Architecture

  • On a write miss, the entire block is loaded from memory before updating the cache
     
  • On a write hit, the block is updated in cache only
     
  • $20 \%$ of the cache blocks are dirty when they are replaced

question.text:
A scalar in-order processor has a base CPI of $1$ in the absence of control hazards. The instruction mix of a program is such that conditional branches are $20$ percent of all instructions and unconditional branches are $5$ percent. The branch target buffer has a hit rate of $80$ percent for both branch types. For conditional branches, when the BTB hits, a $2$-bit saturating counter predictor is used whose direction accuracy is $92$ percent. Unconditional branches are always taken. The actual taken probability of conditional branches is $60$ percent. A direction misprediction incurs a penalty of $5$ cycles. When a branch is taken but the BTB misses, there is a $2$-cycle target resolution penalty even if the direction would have been correct; when a conditional branch is not taken and the BTB misses, there is no penalty. Assume no overlap between penalties and ignore all other stalls.

The average CPI of this processor is _______ (up to $3$ decimal places)

question.text:

I2: ADD R4, R1, R5

I3: SUB R6, R4, R7

  • The processor uses forwarding from the ALU output to the input of subsequent ALU operations.
     
  • Instructions are fetched one per cycle, starting from cycle 1.

Which of the following statements is/are correct?

A. There is a RAW dependency between I1 and I2.

B. After execution of the sequence, the content of the registers is $R 1=-2, R 4=-7, R 6=-11 $

C. 8 stalls are created due to RAW hazard

D. A structural hazard will occur due to the ALU being used by multiple instructions.

question.text:
Consider a processor with byte-addressable memory. All registers, including the Program Counter (PC), Program Status Word (PSW), and Stack Pointer (SP), are $1$ word ($1$ word = $2$ bytes) wide. A stack is implemented in the main memory and grows upward (toward higher addresses).

A CALL instruction occupies $2$ words:

The first word is the opcode and the second word is the starting address of the subroutine. The semantics of CALL (as implemented) are:

  1. Compute the return address = address of the instruction following the CALL.
     
  2. Push the return address onto the stack.
     
  3. Push the PSW onto the stack.
     
  4. Load the starting address of the subroutine into PC.

Push operation:
To push a $2$-byte word W onto the stack:

  • $\mathrm{SP} \leftarrow \mathrm{SP}+2$ (pre-increment because stack grows upward and SP points to top),
     
  • then store the word W at memory addresses SP.

Given:

  • The current content of PC just before fetching the CALL instruction = $0x  1000$ (hex).
  • The two words of the CALL are located at addresses $0x 1000$ (opcode) and $0x 1002$ (operand = starting address).
  • The operand (starting address of subroutine) contained in the CALL is $0x  2000$.
  • The current content of PSW = 0xABCD.
     
  • The current content of $\mathrm{SP}=0x 3006$.

If the machine is Little-Endian, after execution of the CALL, the final values of PC and SP, and the bytes stored at addresses $0x 3008$ through $0 x 300 \mathrm{~B}$ (in increasing address order) will be:

  1. $\mathrm{PC}=0 x 2000, \mathrm{SP}=0 x300A$, bytes $=0410 \mathrm{CD} \mathrm{AB}$
  2. $\mathrm{PC}=0 x 2000, \mathrm{SP}=0 x300A$, bytes $=1004 \mathrm{AB} \mathrm{CD}$
  3. $\mathrm{PC}=0 x 1004, \mathrm{SP}=0 x 300A$, bytes $=0410 \mathrm{CD} \mathrm{AB}$
  4. $\mathrm{PC}=0 x 2000, \mathrm{SP}=0 x 3008$, bytes $=0410 \mathrm{CD} \mathrm{AB}$
question.subject: CO & Architecture

question.text:
A computer architecture uses a 16-bit instruction format. The system designers want to implement the expand opcode technique to increase the number of instructions while supporting multiple addressing modes.

  • The instruction format is divided as follows:
  • Opcode field
  • Addressing mode field
  • Register/Operand field(s)

Two alternative designs are considered:

Design A:

  • Opcode field = 6 bits
     
  • Addressing mode field $=2$ bits
     
  • Register/Operand field $=8$ bits

Design B (Expand Opcode Technique):

  • First 4 bits of the instruction = Primary Opcode.
     
  • If the primary opcode indicates a "special class", then the next 4 bits are used as extended opcode.
     
  • Remaining bits are used for addressing mode (2 bits) and operand (6 bits).
     
  • There are $25 \%$ chances that a primary opcode indicates a special class.

Which of the following options is correct?

  1. Design A supports a greater number of instructions and a larger operand field.
     
  2. Design $B$ supports a greater number of instructions but a smaller operand field.
     
  3. Design A supports a greater number of instructions but a smaller operand field.
     
  4. Design $B$ supports both a greater number of instructions and a larger operand field.

question.text: Suppose a computer has a $4$-way set associative cache with one-word blocks and a total capacity of 256 bytes (word size $=4$ bytes). question.text: A machine has a base CPI of 2 clock cycles. Measurements obtained show that the instruction miss rate is $12 \%$ and the data miss rate is $6 \%$, and that on average, $30 \%$ of all instructions contain one data reference. The miss penalty for the cache is 10 cycles. What is the total CPI?

question.text:
A block-set-associative cache consists of $64$ blocks divided into $4$-block sets.
The main memory has $4096$ blocks, each block containing $32$ words.
Assuming:

  • The machine has a $32$-bit byte-addressable address space
  • Word size $=4$ bytes

How many bits are there in each of the Tag, Set, and Word/Byte offset fields?

  1. Tag $=21$ bits, Set $=4$ bits, Word/Byte offset $=7$ bits
     
  2. Tag $=20$ bits, Set $=5$ bits, Word/Byte offset $=7$ bits
     
  3. Tag $=21$ bits, Set $=5$ bits, Word/Byte offset $=6$ bits
     
  4. Tag $=22$ bits, Set $=4$ bits, Word/Byte offset $=6$ bits
question.subject: CO & Architecture

question.text:

  1. Data hazards can sometimes be resolved using forwarding (bypassing)
  2. Structural hazards occur when two instructions require the same hardware resource at the same time
  3. Control hazards are completely eliminated by instruction pipelining
  4. Read After Write (RAW), Write After Read (WAR), and Write After Write (WAW) are all types of data hazards
